summary: Wooden pierhead lighthouse at the mouth of the Twin Rivers: lit 1886, deactivated 1969, moved to the Rogers Street museum in 1975, lens restored and unveiled 2009.

lens.note: Sixth-order Fresnel lens by Sautter & Co., red light (LighthouseFriends). The museum describes a 240-degree Fresnel lens; the restored lens is on display (museum).

structures.type: square pyramidal timber tower with lantern
structures.note: 35 ft from base to ventilator ball (LighthouseFriends). Moved in 1975 from the north pier to the museum grounds (LighthouseFriends; museum). USLHS gives tower material wood and shape square.

structures.type: duplex for two keepers (enlarged existing house)
structures.note: Congress funded a keeper's dwelling by act of February 25, 1907. The Board bought and enlarged an existing residence; LighthouseFriends says the work was finished in September 1908 (printed as 19018). Oil house built 1909.

structures.name: Twin Rivers light
structures.type: one-and-a-half-story brick dwelling with octagonal lantern
structures.note: On the point at the river mouth; discontinued August 1859 (LighthouseFriends). What became of the brick structure is not stated.

facts.agency: Rogers Street Fishing Village and Great Lakes Coast Guard Museum (holds the tower)

access.note: Museum grounds; the museum says visitors can climb the tower. Hours not checked.

visit.note: Restored lens on display; the museum offers to flash the light on a chosen date in memory or honor of someone.

events.note: Congress appropriated $3,500 for a lighthouse at the mouth of the Twin Rivers.
Work began on a brick dwelling with an octagonal lantern for the Twin Rivers light; land deed obtained April 1852.
Sixth-order Fresnel lens in the lantern of the Twin Rivers light by 1858.
Twin Rivers light discontinued in August 1859 under the Board's 1859 authority to discontinue useless lights.
Pierhead light authorized for Two Rivers; no contract until 1886.
Contract June 22, 1886 with a Manitowoc builder (Boehmer); completed October 14, 1886 at the end of the north pier, with 1,315 ft of elevated walkway.
Pierhead light first lit on the night of October 25, 1886 by Keeper Antony Gauthier.
November 1886: a vessel driven into the pier damaged the light and walkway; repairs made at once.

Board reports for fiscal 1895 describe a separate light at Twin River Point, where an iron tower built from parts of an old Chicago River light was being erected on eight columns. Not the pierhead light; LighthouseFriends does not mention it.
Act of February 25, 1907 funded a keeper's dwelling (LighthouseFriends).
Duplex keeper's dwelling finished September 1908 (LighthouseFriends prints 19018).
1,500-pound fog bell mounted on the seaward side of the tower, struck by a Gamewell apparatus wound by a motor.
Sanford Scott hired as first assistant keeper to operate the fog bell.
Diaphone fog signal installed; light changed to electric illuminant (LighthouseFriends).
Storm damage from wave action to the north side of the tower (about 30 ft high); repaired (museum).
Deactivated and replaced by a modern beacon; USLHS gives 1969 as the year discontinued.
Upper portion of the wooden tower moved onto the grounds of the Rogers Street Fishing Village at Rogers Street and 21st Street; the lens was broken in the move.
Wide wooden walkway built around the relocated tower.
Restored Fresnel lens unveiled May 28, 2009 after a restoration begun in 2005 (museum).

corrections.why: The record's point is the 1975 museum site on Rogers Street (current coordinates of the relocated tower). The 1886 to 1969 pierhead stood at the end of the north pier; the USLHS gives 44 8.34 N, 87 33.37 W (44.139, -87.5562). Keep the museum point as the tower's present position if the record needs one.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS lists the 1853 to 1859 keepers (Ruggles, Barry, Ward) under the pierhead record. LighthouseFriends ties them to the 1852 Twin Rivers light, which the pierhead replaced. The keepers are attributed here to the 1852 light.
LighthouseFriends prints the completion year of the keeper's duplex as 19018. Read as 1908 from context (the 1907 act and the 1909 oil house).

LighthouseFriends says $7,400 was requested from 1919. The Commissioner's 1919 estimate asks $6,000 for the Two Rivers light and fog signal; the 1920 estimate asks $7,400, and the same figure appears in the next two reports.

notes_for_editor: Two Rivers has two lights in the sources and the record covers one. The Board's reports of the 1890s list a 'Twin River Point' light (fiscal 1895: an iron tower built from parts of an old Chicago River light on eight columns; fiscal 1896-97: removal of the old tower and an oil house moved to a line with the iron tower; the 1894 move is at scan pages 25 and 45, fiscal 1895 at scan page 342, and 1896-97 at scan page 145). LighthouseFriends says the 1852 light was discontinued in 1859 and does not mention these reports. The story says the two accounts cannot be reconciled from the sources read. A person should decide whether the Twin River Point light needs its own record and whether this record's history should carry it. The Lighthouse Board corpus stops at fiscal 1901, so 1886 to 1901 pierhead details come only from LighthouseFriends; the 1886 collision is not confirmed in a primary source. Wikipedia (not cited) gives the 1852 light as 1852 to 1858 and says the pierhead was tended from the Rawley Point light; both conflict with LighthouseFriends and the USLHS and were not used. The museum calls the 1886 tower one of few original wooden structures on the Great Lakes and says wooden construction was largely replaced by 1900 for reasons including the 1928 damage; that last claim does not fit a wooden tower of 1886 still standing, and it is not used. The museum's Life-Saving Station (commissioned 1877) and the Life-Saving Service Station No. 17 reports (1878 to 1882) are different structures and are not used for this light. The museum's National Register claim for the complex was not checked against the NPS database. Visitor hours were not checked; the museum's home page says visitors can climb the tower. Current ownership is not settled: the record says unknown; the museum holds the tower. Chronicling America was not searched for the 1886 collision. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the story states the disagreement over the fog-signal request. LighthouseFriends dates the $7,400 request to 1919, but the Commissioner's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1919 gives $6,000; the $7,400 estimate appears in the reports for the fiscal years ended June 30, 1920, 1921 and 1922 (scan pages 581, 692 and 777 of the bound Commissioner volume). The 1921 OCR prints Two Rivera; the quote is kept as printed. The 1895 Board entry is on scan pages 342 and 343 (the eight-column foundations are on page 343). The 1909 dwelling completion is printed 19018 by LighthouseFriends; the story reads 1908 from context (1907 act, 1909 oil house), as recorded in resolved_conflicts. Feet are converted in the story (US units first with metres in brackets).
